sections.abstract: DICE is the first end-to-end method for Deformation-aware hand-face Interaction reCovEry from a single image. Reconstructing these interactions is challenging due to self-occlusions, diverse spatial relationships, and complex deformations. Unlike the previous state-of-the-art, Decaf, which relies on time-consuming global fitting optimization (over 15 seconds per image), DICE estimates hand and face poses, contacts, and deformations simultaneously using a Transformer-based architecture. The model disentangles the regression of local deformation fields and global mesh vertex locations into two network branches. To enhance generalization, DICE employs a weakly-supervised training approach for in-the-wild images using depth priors from off-the-shelf models and adversarial priors for poses. Experiments show DICE achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks and in-the-wild data, operating at an interactive rate of 20 fps on an Nvidia 4090 GPU.
sections.introduction: Hand-face interaction is a frequent human behavior (up to 800 times daily), making its 3D reconstruction vital for AR/VR, animation, and behavior analysis. Challenges include self-occlusions, diverse poses/contacts, and single-view ambiguity. Most existing methods either ignore contacts and deformations or are too slow for interactive use. DICE addresses these issues with three key designs: 1) a Transformer-based model to capture hand-face relationships; 2) disentangled regression of global geometry and local interaction; and 3) an intermediate non-parametric mesh representation used to regress parametric model parameters via a neural inverse-kinematics (IK) network. To overcome the limited diversity of studio-collected datasets, DICE introduces a weak-supervision pipeline for in-the-wild images, leveraging depth priors from diffusion-based models and adversarial pose priors from separate hand/face datasets. The result is a model that surpasses previous regression and optimization-based methods in accuracy, physical plausibility, and speed.
sections.method: The paper reviews three main areas: 1) 3D Interacting Hands Recovery, noting the shift from fitting frameworks to regression-based approaches and the unique challenge of modeling interactions with a deformable face; 2) 3D Human Face Recovery, where most literature neglects the face's deformable nature during hand-face interactions; and 3) 3D Full-Body Recovery, which typically focuses on the main body with only rough estimations for hands and face. DICE distinguishes itself by uniquely accounting for detailed, non-rigid interactions and deformations between these components in an end-to-end manner. The task is to reconstruct hand mesh vertices $V_H \in \mathbb{R}^{778 \times 3}$, face mesh vertices $V_F \in \mathbb{R}^{5023 \times 3}$, face deformation vectors $D \in \mathbb{R}^{5023 \times 3}$, and per-vertex contact probabilities $C_H \in \mathbb{R}^{778}$ and $C_F \in \mathbb{R}^{5023}$ from a single RGB image $I$. DICE uses an HRNet-W64 backbone to extract a feature map $F \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (C+3)}$, where $N$ corresponds to keypoints and downsampled vertices. This map is fed into two branches: MeshNet (regressing unrefined vertex positions $V'_H$ and $V'_F$) and InteractionNet (predicting deformation field $D$ and contact labels $C_H, C_F$). An IKNet then takes $V'_H$ and $V'_F$ to predict parametric model parameters: $(\theta_h, \beta_h)$ for MANO (hand) and $(\theta_{f-pose}, \beta_f, \theta_{f-exp})$ for FLAME (face). The final face mesh is $V_F = V^*_F + D$. \n\nWeakly-supervised training utilizes in-the-wild images with pseudo-ground-truth from 2D keypoint detectors and the Marigold depth estimator. Depth supervision uses a modified SILog loss: $\mathcal{L}_{depth} = [\mathbf{Var}(\log(K_D + \varepsilon) - \log(\hat{K}_D + \varepsilon))]^{1/2}$. Adversarial priors $\mathcal{L}_{adv}$ are applied to predicted parameters to ensure plausibility. The total loss is: $\mathcal{L} = \lambda_{mesh}\mathcal{L}_{mesh} + \lambda_{interaction}\mathcal{L}_{interaction} + \lambda_{adv}\mathcal{L}_{adv} + \lambda_{depth}\mathcal{L}_{depth}$, with weights $\lambda_{mesh}=12.5, \lambda_{interaction}=5, \lambda_{depth}=2.5, \lambda_{adv}=1$.
sections.experiments: DICE is evaluated on the Decaf dataset and a custom in-the-wild dataset of 500 images. Metrics include MPJPE, PAMPJPE, PVE, Collision Distance (Col. Dist.), Non-Collision Ratio (Non. Col.), Touchness Ratio, and F-Score. Implementation involves AdamW optimizers with a learning rate of $6 \times 10^{-4}$ over 40 epochs on 8 Nvidia A6000 GPUs. Baselines include Decaf (optimization-based), PIXIE (whole-body), METRO, and FastMETRO.
sections.results: Quantitative results show DICE achieves a 7.5% reduction in per-vertex error compared to Decaf and a 27% MPVE reduction compared to PIXIE-R. DICE also demonstrates superior contact estimation performance (F-score of 0.61 for face and 0.50 for hand). Qualitative results highlight DICE's robustness to self-occlusion and its ability to generalize to in-the-wild scenarios where previous methods often fail or produce artifacts. DICE outperforms all baseline methods in reconstruction accuracy and physical plausibility. It achieves the best results in PVE (8.32), MPJPE (9.95), and PAMPJPE (7.27) on the Decaf benchmark. While some optimization-based methods show higher physical plausibility metrics due to iterative adjustment, DICE remains the best among regression-based models and even outperforms the Benchmark optimization method in F-score. Crucially, DICE operates at 20 fps (0.049s per image), which is over 200x faster than Decaf's optimization process. Ablation studies confirm that the two-branch architecture, depth supervision, and adversarial priors are essential for accurate z-direction recovery and avoiding self-penetration artifacts.
sections.conclusion: The paper presents DICE, the first end-to-end approach for capturing 3D hand-face interactions and deformations from monocular images. By utilizing a two-branch Transformer architecture, an IKNet for parametric mesh output, and a novel weak-supervision pipeline with depth and adversarial priors, DICE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalization. It runs at interactive speeds (20 fps), making it suitable for real-time applications. Future work will focus on improving deformation accuracy and exploring physics-based simulations for even more realistic results.
sections.supplementary: Appendix A: Implementation Details. The CNN backbone is HRNet-W64. MeshNet and InteractionNet use progressive downsampling transformer encoders with 4 layers and 4 attention heads. IKNet consists of five MLP blocks with skip connections and hidden dimensions of 1024. Appendix B: More Qualitative Comparisons. Demonstrates that depth loss is critical for eliminating z-direction ambiguity and preventing self-penetration. Appendix C: Addition Details on Losses. Mesh loss $\mathcal{L}_{mesh} = \mathcal{L}_{reproj} + 4\mathcal{L}_{vert} + 2\mathcal{L}_{key} + 2\mathcal{L}_{params}$. Interaction loss $\mathcal{L}_{interaction} = 0.2\mathcal{L}_{touch} + 0.6\mathcal{L}_{contact} + \mathcal{L}_{collision} + 6\mathcal{L}_{deform}$. The deformation loss is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{deform} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} (1 + \mu \|\hat{d_i}\|_2)\|\hat{d_i} - d_i\|_2^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \mathcal{L}} \|d_i\|$, where $\mu=5000$ and $\lambda=100$. Appendix D: More Discussions. DICE is robust under challenging self-occlusion (e.g., hand covering half the face). Failure cases occur during complete occlusion or with out-of-distribution data (e.g., infants, gloves). The authors address societal impacts, warning against potential misuse for deepfakes and emphasizing the need for data fairness in future dataset collection.
